1 Summary

About this paper. The text, analysis, figures and simulations were written by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, at the direction of Robert Drzyzgula, who set its scope and questions. It is the second companion to Speed Control of Universal Motors in Sewing Machines (cited here as “the speed-control paper”). The first companion, Inside the Motor, looks inside the motors. This one looks inside the switches that control them. The sources are listed in the last section; please report errors as issues on the project’s GitHub repository.

Research use only: not a safe, buildable design. The motor-control circuits, schematics, enclosures, mechanisms, test procedures and software in this project have not been safety-designed, safety-validated, certified, or tested as a complete appliance. None of the controller designs should be built or connected to the mains as drawn, and none should be operated. A concept drawing, simulation, component listing, historical example or commercial component is not evidence of compliance or safety; printed plastic is not an assessed insulation system or fire enclosure, and a barrier drawn on a schematic is not proof of isolation. The work is meant to support understanding of how existing and historical controls work and what hazards they carry, and to guide the development of safer alternatives. It is personal learning done in public, not a product, and anyone who uses or builds on any of it does so on their own responsibility. Any future buildable design would need a new system- level engineering assessment, independent review, qualified implementation, complete-product testing and applicable certification; docs/VALIDATION.md lists what that would cover. This paper studies how existing switching circuits work; explaining a circuit is not recommending it. Its curves and figures are simulations from assumed component and motor values, not measurements, and are not evidence of performance or safety.

What it covers. The speed-control paper treats a phase-control pedal as a box that chops the line: it sets a firing angle, and the motor gets part of each half-cycle. This paper opens the box.

  • The thyristor (SCR). It starts with the device the others grew from: four layers of silicon that latch on when their gate is pulsed and stay on until the current stops. It explains why it latches, with the two-transistor model, and the ways it can be turned on that nobody intended.
  • The triac and the diac. A triac is two thyristors in one piece of silicon, back to back, so it conducts both ways. It covers how it fires in four “quadrants”, why it is harder to turn off than two separate SCRs, and how the diac gives it a clean trigger.
  • Phase control. A minimal pedal circuit, part by part: how its RC network sets the firing angle, why the circuit remembers the last half-cycle, and why that memory makes a pedal snap on.
  • The snubber. What the little resistor and capacitor across a triac are for, why some triacs don’t need them, and why one might be fitted anyway.
  • The donor board. The KB3151C pedal board that the VSM Base’s knee controller reuses, worked through in detail: its pot and trimmer in parallel, and what its minimum-speed trimmer does to the pedal’s feel, simulated across its range.
  • Switches a gate can turn off. Power MOSFETs, IGBTs and their relatives: how they differ from thyristors, why a cordless drill uses one kind and a variable-frequency drive another, and what that means for leading-edge and trailing-edge control.
  • Where each appears in the project. The knee controller, the MCU controller and its two DC variants, and the KB Electronics controllers the speed-control paper discusses.

The short answers.

  1. A thyristor is a latch. Its four layers form two transistors, each feeding the other’s base. A gate pulse starts the loop, and once the current is large enough the loop holds itself on. Only stopping the current resets it. On AC the line does that every half-cycle, which is why thyristors and phase control grew up together.
  2. A triac is two thyristors sharing silicon, and it pays for that in turn-off. One gate fires it either way. But when the current reverses it has no time to recover between the two directions. A fast-rising voltage just after a current zero can turn it straight back on. Inductive loads such as a motor cause exactly that.
  3. In a pedal, a resistor and a capacitor are the clock. The capacitor charges through the pedal’s resistance, lagging the line, until it reaches the diac’s breakover, about 32 V. More resistance means later firing and less voltage. Past about 137 kΩ with 0.1 µF it never fires. The capacitor carries charge from one half-cycle to the next. That memory is why the motor starts at about 40% of the line’s voltage and then runs slower than it would start.
  4. The snubber slows the voltage edge that would otherwise re-fire the triac after an inductive turn-off. Triacs built for inductive loads (“snubberless”) can do without it, at the cost of a less sensitive gate.
  5. The donor board’s trimmer sets where in the pedal’s travel the motor snaps on, not how gently. Set high, it leaves a quarter of the travel dead. Set near 430 kΩ, the motor starts as soon as the pedal leaves its off zone. Set below the pot’s own 200 kΩ, the pedal stops being monotonic.
  6. Transistor switches turn off on command. That makes PWM and trailing-edge control possible, and with them DC motor drives, VFDs and brakes. MOSFETs rule at low voltage and high speed, as in the cordless drill. IGBTs rule at mains-derived voltages and kilowatts, as in a VFD or an industrial servo. Thyristors survive where the line does the turning off for free.

On the simulations. The firing curves are computed from a simple model of the timing network, not measured. It uses a 32 V breakover, 22 V left on the capacitor after firing, a 120 V line and a resistive load. The voltage left after firing is the least certain of these. The motor test rig is meant to measure the real board, and its results should replace these figures.

2 The thyristor (SCR)

The silicon-controlled rectifier, or SCR, is the oldest of the power switches in this paper and the parent of the triac. “Thyristor” is the family name; in everyday use it means the SCR. Bell Labs worked out the four-layer PNPN device in the mid-1950s, and General Electric brought the SCR to market in 1957. Within a few years it had replaced the thyratron tube and the magnetic amplifier in motor drives, lamp dimmers and battery chargers. It is still the cheapest way to switch large currents from an AC line.

2.1 Four layers, two transistors

An SCR is a sandwich of four alternately doped layers: P, N, P, N. The outer P layer is the anode, the outer N layer the cathode, and the gate connects to the inner P layer next to the cathode.

The structure has three junctions, J1, J2 and J3. With the anode positive, J1 and J3 are forward biased, but J2 in the middle is reverse biased and blocks. With the anode negative, J1 and J3 block. So an SCR that has not been triggered blocks in both directions.

The key to the device is to see the four layers as two transistors that share their middle layers, as the figure shows: a PNP made of the first three layers and an NPN made of the last three. The PNP’s collector is the NPN’s base, and the NPN’s collector is the PNP’s base. Each transistor’s output current is the other’s input.

Call the two transistors’ common-base current gains α1\alpha_1 (PNP) and α2\alpha_2 (NPN), the fraction of each one’s emitter current that reaches its collector. Summing the currents at the junctions gives the anode current:

IA=α2IG+ICO1+ICO21−(α1+α2)I_A = \frac{\alpha_2 I_G + I_{CO1} + I_{CO2}}{1 - (\alpha_1 + \alpha_2)}

Here IGI_G is the gate current and the ICOI_{CO} terms are the two transistors’ small leakage currents. In silicon, α\alpha is small at tiny currents and rises with current. With no gate current, the sum α1+α2\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 is well below 1 and only leakage flows: the SCR is off. A pulse of gate current raises the NPN’s current and so its α\alpha. That sends more current into the PNP’s base, which raises its α\alpha, and so on. When α1+α2\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 reaches 1, the denominator goes to zero: the loop gain is one, and the current is limited only by the external circuit. The SCR has switched on, and it stays on with no gate current at all.

Why should α\alpha rise with current? At low current densities, much of the emitter current is lost to recombination, at defects in the junctions’ depletion regions and at the surface, before it can cross the base. That loss grows only slowly with current, so as the current rises, a larger share of it gets through. Designers use this. The emitters are shorted to the P layer next to them in places, so that small currents (leakage, or the displacement current of a fast voltage edge) bypass the emitter entirely and can’t start the loop. Only a real gate current, or a large enough fault, raises the gains to one.

The layers’ doping sets the voltages. The N1 layer next to the anode is thick and lightly doped, because the blocking junction’s depletion region spreads into it: the thicker and purer it is, the higher the voltage it holds off. It is also where the stored charge sits when the device conducts, which is why high-voltage thyristors are slower to turn off.

2.2 Latching and holding

Two currents describe the latch:

  • Latching current, ILI_L. The anode current must reach this before the gate pulse ends, or the loop gain falls below one and the SCR drops out. It matters with inductive loads, where the current rises slowly after firing.
  • Holding current, IHI_H. Once latched, the SCR stays on until the anode current falls below this, a few milliamps for a small device. Then the loop gain falls below one and it turns off.

The gate can start the regenerative loop but can’t stop it. A negative gate current large enough to steal the loop’s own current would turn it off, but for an ordinary SCR that is about the whole anode current. The gate turn-off thyristor (GTO) is built to make that practical; §7 comes back to it.

So an SCR is turned off by commutation: something outside it brings its current to zero. On an AC line, the line does that every half-cycle (“natural” or “line” commutation). After the current stops, the SCR also needs a short time with no forward voltage, its turn-off time tqt_q, tens of microseconds for a phase-control part, to sweep the stored charge out of its middle layers. Apply forward voltage sooner and it turns back on. Early DC choppers and inverters had to force commutation with extra capacitors and SCRs, and the circuitry was elaborate; transistor switches retired them (§7).

2.3 Ways to turn it on, intended and not

Any current that drives the loop gain to one fires an SCR. The gate is the intended way, but there are others:

  • Breakover. Raise the forward voltage far enough and J2’s leakage avalanches until the loop latches. This is the breakover voltage, well above the device’s rating. The diac (§3) is built to work this way on purpose.
  • Rate of rise of voltage (dV/dt). The blocking junction J2 is a capacitor. A forward voltage rising at dV/dtdV/dt drives a current CdV/dtC\,dV/dt through it, which acts exactly like gate current. Fast enough, and the SCR fires with no gate signal. Datasheets give the critical dV/dtdV/dt. Snubbers (§5) exist largely to stay under it.
  • Temperature. Leakage roughly doubles every 10 °C or so, so a hot SCR needs less to fire and holds on at lower currents.
  • Light. Photons absorbed near J2 make carriers too. Light-triggered thyristors fire this way deliberately, in high-voltage DC converters, and the opto-triacs in §3 use the same idea.

There is also a limit on how fast the current may rise once it fires, dI/dtdI/dt. Conduction starts in a small region near the gate and spreads across the chip over microseconds. A current that rises too fast crowds into that region and can burn it.

2.4 What SCRs are used for

An SCR conducts in one direction only, so on AC it gives controlled rectification: DC whose average is set by the firing angle. The classic uses:

  • DC motor drives. A bridge with SCRs in some or all of its arms turns the line into adjustable DC for a permanent-magnet or shunt-wound motor. This is how the KB Electronics KBIC controllers discussed in the speed-control paper (§8 there) work, with feedback from the armature.
  • AC phase control with two SCRs connected inverse-parallel, one for each half-cycle. In large industrial heaters and soft starters this pair is still preferred over a triac, because each SCR has a whole half-cycle to recover.
  • Crowbars, which short a power supply’s output when it goes over voltage, so that a fuse blows instead of the load.
  • Chargers, welders and high-voltage DC links, at sizes up to whole power stations.

For a sewing-machine pedal, though, the useful step was putting two SCRs into one chip with one gate: the triac.

3 The triac and the diac

3.1 Two thyristors in one chip

A triac is, in effect, two SCRs connected inverse-parallel and built into a single piece of silicon with a single gate. General Electric introduced it in the 1960s, for lamp dimmers and appliance controls. Because it conducts either way, its main terminals aren’t called anode and cathode. They are MT1, the terminal the gate is referenced to, and MT2. On a TO-220 package such as the BT136, MT2 is the metal tab, so the tab is live.

Inside, it is one chip with two SCRs folded together. The figure shows the layout. The thick, lightly doped N1 layer in the middle blocks the voltage in both directions, as in an SCR. Above and below it are P2 and P1. The N-type emitters are let into the outer faces at different places:

  • N2, under MT1, makes P1–N1–P2–N2, an SCR that conducts from MT2 to MT1 when MT2 is positive. This is the left-hand path in the figure.
  • N4, under MT2, on the opposite side of the chip, makes P2–N1–P1–N4, an SCR the other way up, conducting from MT1 to MT2 when MT2 is negative. It sits under the part of MT1 that touches P2 directly.
  • N3, under the gate, is a small emitter beside the gate’s contact to P2. It is what lets a negative gate current fire the triac (below).

Each terminal’s metal touches both an N emitter and the P layer beside it. That is a deliberate short. It keeps the emitters from injecting until a real gate or load current flows, which is what sets the triac’s sensitivity and its dV/dt rating.

The triac behaves as described for the SCR: it latches, the gate can’t turn it off, and it turns off when the current through it falls below the holding current. So all a control circuit can choose is when to switch it on in each half-cycle. That moment is the firing angle α\alpha, measured from the voltage zero. This is leading-edge (or forward-phase) control:

  • The line crosses zero. The triac is off, and stays off.
  • At α\alpha the gate is pulsed, and the triac switches the line onto the load. A larger α\alpha means a later start and less power.
  • The current reaches zero, and the triac turns itself off until the next pulse.

With a resistive load the current reaches zero with the voltage. A motor is inductive, so its current lags and the triac stays on a little past the voltage zero. Inside the Motor (§3 there) shows the motor current behind a triac in detail.

3.2 Four quadrants

A triac can be fired with gate current of either sign, whichever way MT2 is biased. That gives four combinations, called quadrants:

Quadrant MT2, relative to MT1 Gate current BT136-600E: gate current to fire (typ / max)
I positive positive, into the gate 2.5 / 10 mA
II positive negative, out of the gate 4 / 10 mA
III negative negative 5 / 10 mA
IV negative positive 11 / 25 mA

The four work by different routes through the structure, which is why they aren’t equally easy:

  • Quadrant I is an ordinary SCR’s gate. Current from the gate flows through P2 to N2, forward-biases the P2–N2 junction, and the left-hand SCR fires.
  • Quadrant II uses the gate’s own emitter. With the gate negative, N3 injects electrons into P2. That turns on a small auxiliary SCR, P1–N1–P2–N3, under the gate first. Its current flows sideways through P2 to MT1, and acts as a large gate current for the main SCR, which fires next. The auxiliary SCR is a built-in amplifier.
  • Quadrant III is a “remote gate”. With MT2 negative, the SCR to fire is the right-hand one, which has no gate of its own. Electrons injected by N3 cross P2 into N1. There they lower N1’s potential and act as base current for the PNP section, P2–N1–P1, which turns the right-hand SCR on.
  • Quadrant IV is the most indirect. Positive gate current forward-biases P2–N2 under MT1, and N2 injects electrons that have to find their way to N1 to fire the right-hand SCR, the far side of the chip. Little of the gate’s effort gets there, so it needs the most gate current and fires the slowest.

Circuits avoid quadrant IV where they can:

  • A diac-triggered pedal fires in I and III. The timing capacitor charges with the same sign as MT2, so the gate pulse has the same sign too.
  • A microcontroller running at line potential, as in many appliance controllers, usually drives the gate negative in both half-cycles. That is quadrants II and III, both sensitive, and it needs only one supply polarity.
  • “Three-quadrant” triacs, such as ST’s Snubberless and NXP’s Hi-Com types, don’t fire in quadrant IV at all. In exchange they turn off inductive loads far better (§5).

3.3 Why a triac is harder to turn off than two SCRs

In an inverse-parallel pair, each SCR conducts for one half-cycle and then has the whole next half-cycle, 8 ms, to recover while the other one carries the current. In a triac the same silicon carries both directions. When the current falls to zero at the end of one half-cycle, the region that just conducted is still full of carriers. The voltage across the triac is about to rise in the opposite direction, and that direction belongs to the other half of the same chip. If the voltage rises fast enough, the leftover carriers act like gate current and the triac turns straight back on, now in the other direction.

So triac datasheets add two ratings:

  • the commutating dV/dt, (dV/dt)c(dV/dt)_c, the fastest rise of reapplied voltage that the triac will block after conducting;
  • the commutating dI/dt, (dI/dt)c(dI/dt)_c, the fastest fall of current through zero that it can turn off from. A current that falls fast leaves more carriers behind.

With a resistive load the voltage rises gently from zero after the current stops, and neither rating matters. With a motor, the current reaches zero after the voltage, so the line is already tens of volts into the next half-cycle. That voltage appears across the triac within microseconds. This is the case the snubber in §5 is for.

3.4 The diac

A diac is a three-layer, two-terminal trigger, symmetrical, with no gate. In effect it is a transistor with no base connection, built with both junctions alike so that it works the same either way round.

With voltage across it, one junction is forward-biased and the other reverse-biased. Almost nothing flows until the reverse-biased junction reaches its avalanche voltage, about 32 V for the common DB3 (28–36 V). The avalanche current flows into the floating middle layer, where it acts as base current. The transistor’s gain rises with current, as an SCR’s does (§2), so the more current flows, the less voltage it takes to keep it flowing. That is a negative resistance: past breakover, the voltage falls back by at least 5 V (the “breakback”) as the current rises, until the device is conducting heavily at a lower voltage.

That snap is the point. A capacitor charged to 32 V dumps part of its charge through the diac into the triac’s gate as a short, sharp pulse of current, far more than the gate needs. Unlike an SCR, a diac doesn’t latch: it has no fourth layer, so when the capacitor’s current falls away, it stops conducting.

Why not feed the gate straight from the capacitor through a resistor? The gate fires at a fraction of a volt and a few milliamps, so it would fire on a slowly rising, poorly defined current that varies with temperature and from one triac to the next. The diac waits for a definite voltage, then delivers a definite pulse. The firing point is set by the RC network and the diac, not by the triac’s gate sensitivity.

3.5 Other ways to fire a triac

  • Opto-triacs (MOC3020 to MOC3023, and others) put a small light-triggered triac in a package with an LED. They fire the main triac’s gate from an isolated, low-voltage circuit, such as a microcontroller. The MCU design in the speed-control paper uses a MOC3023. Zero-crossing versions (MOC3041 to MOC3043) only fire near the voltage zero, which suits switching heaters on and off. They can’t do phase control.
  • Pulse transformers isolate the gate drive magnetically. They are common in industrial SCR drives.
  • Solid-state relays package an opto-coupler and a triac (or two SCRs) together. Most switch at the zero crossing and are on-off switches, not phase controls. “Random-turn-on” versions exist for phase control.

4 Phase control: a pedal circuit, part by part

4.1 The minimal circuit

The figure strips a phase-control pedal to its essentials, without the extra parts of a real board such as the donor board in §6.

The triac sits in series with the motor, as §3 describes. While it is off, it holds off the whole line and the motor gets nothing.

The timing network is VR, R and C, connected across the triac. While the triac is off, the network sees the whole line voltage. The motor in series drops almost nothing, since the network draws well under a milliamp. C charges through VR + R, and its voltage lags the line and is smaller than it. In steady state it is the line voltage divided by 1+(ωRC)2\sqrt{1 + (\omega RC)^2} and delayed by arctan(ωRC)\arctan(\omega RC):

vC=Vpk1+(ωRC)2sin(ωt−arctanωRC)v_C = \frac{V_{pk}}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega RC)^2}}\,\sin\!\left(\omega t - \arctan \omega RC\right)

Here RR is VR + R, and ω=2π×60\omega = 2\pi \times 60. With 106 kΩ and 0.1 µF, ωRC=4.0\omega RC = 4.0, so C swings to 41 V peak, lagging the line by 76°. Turning VR up both shrinks this voltage and delays it, so it reaches the diac’s breakover later in the half-cycle. Past a certain point its peak no longer reaches the breakover at all, and nothing fires. On 120 V, setting Vpk/1+(ωRC)2=32V_{pk}/\sqrt{1 + (\omega RC)^2} = 32 V gives ωRC=5.2\omega RC = 5.2. That is RC=13.8RC = 13.8 ms, about 137 kΩ with 0.1 µF. It is where a pedal’s motor starts.

The diac fires the triac when C reaches about 32 V, in quadrant I on the positive half-cycle and quadrant III on the negative (§3).

R, in series with VR, keeps the total resistance from reaching zero. It limits the current through the pot’s wiper and track at the full-speed end, and so sets the earliest firing. Even with VR at zero, C still has to reach 32 V while the line rises, so the circuit fires a little after the line passes 32 V: about 11° into the half-cycle, essentially full voltage.

4.2 The firing angle and the circuit’s memory

Each half-cycle, C charges until it reaches the diac’s breakover. The diac then fires the triac, and the triac conducts until the motor current falls to zero. That happens a little after the voltage zero, because the motor is inductive. Delaying the firing angle α\alpha reduces the share of each half-cycle applied to the motor. For a resistive load, the RMS output is:

Vrms=Vpk12π(π−α+12sin2α)V_{rms} = V_{pk}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\pi}\left(\pi - \alpha + \tfrac{1}{2}\sin 2\alpha\right)}

The motor’s inductance stretches the conduction past the voltage zero, so the real curve differs, but the shape holds: a smooth fall from full voltage at α=0\alpha = 0 to nothing at α=π\alpha = \pi.

The bottom panel of the figure shows that the circuit has a memory. When the diac fires, it leaves C at about 22 V. With the triac on, the network sees only the triac’s volt or so across it, so C drains slowly through VR + R. It still holds about 15 V of the same sign when the line reverses. The next half-cycle has to pull it back through zero before charging it the other way. A capacitor that has not been firing starts each half-cycle further back: at about −30 V near the start threshold, the trough of the plain RC’s lagging sine.

4.3 Snap-on hysteresis

That difference is why a simple pedal snaps on. The setting that starts the motor is not the one that stops it:

  • Starting. In the model, the motor starts when VR + R falls to about 137 kΩ. The first firing comes late in the half-cycle, but it leaves C partly discharged, so the next one comes earlier. Within a few cycles the firing angle settles at about 125°, roughly 40% of the line’s RMS voltage. The motor jumps from stopped to a brisk speed.
  • Running. Once running, it keeps firing as the resistance rises, until about 158 kΩ, near 155° and roughly a tenth of the line.

So the pedal needs a push to start, the motor jumps to a speed above where you wanted it, and then it will run slower than it would start. The jump happens near 125° whatever the pot’s value, because it comes from the capacitor’s memory. A different pot or trimmer only moves where in the pedal’s travel it happens (§6).

Two-stage networks reduce the jump. A second resistor and capacitor feed the timing capacitor from a node that is itself an RC delay of the line. After each firing, that second capacitor recharges the timing capacitor from a defined voltage, so the timing capacitor starts each half-cycle from nearly the same place whether or not the last one fired. The memory, and with it most of the hysteresis, is erased. Lamp-dimmer and tool-speed application notes have used this since the 1960s; better pedals do it, and cheap ones don’t.

4.4 A little accidental feedback

Before the triac fires, the RC network charges from the voltage across the triac. That is the line voltage minus the small back-EMF the turning armature generates from residual field magnetism. A slowing motor makes less back-EMF, so the capacitor charges slightly faster and fires earlier, which speeds the motor back up. The effect is small in a simple pedal. Exploiting it deliberately, with the network arranged to sense the armature’s voltage, is the basis of the regulated designs in the speed-control paper (§7 there).

4.5 The model behind the figures

The simulation is in tools/make_triac_figures.py. Within each half-cycle it solves the RC network exactly (a capacitor charged through a resistor from a sine), and it carries the capacitor’s voltage from one half-cycle to the next, so the start and stop thresholds come out of the model rather than being put in. Its assumptions:

  • a 120 V, 60 Hz line;
  • before firing, the whole line across the triac; after it, about 1 V until the half-cycle ends;
  • a resistive load, so the triac turns off at the voltage zero;
  • a 32 V breakover, with the capacitor dropping to 22 V when the diac fires. A DB3 breaks over anywhere from 28 to 36 V and falls back by at least 5 V; the voltage left after firing is the least certain number.

5 The snubber

The snubber, Rs in series with Cs straight across the triac (the dashed box in §4’s figure), is there for the moment the triac turns off. §3 explained the problem: a fast-rising voltage across a triac can turn it on, either just after it has conducted (commutating dV/dt) or at any time (static dV/dt).

5.1 What can go wrong without one

Commutation. With a resistive load, the current reaches zero together with the voltage, so the voltage across the triac grows gently from zero. A motor is inductive: its current lags. By the time the current has fallen to zero and the triac turns off, the line is already some way into the next half-cycle, at tens of volts of the opposite polarity. That voltage appears across the triac at once, limited only by stray capacitance: a step of many volts per microsecond. The triac, still full of charge carriers, turns straight back on and conducts the whole next half-cycle, whatever the timing network wanted. Control is lost, and the motor runs on at full speed or lurches.

Static dV/dt. Even a triac that has been off for some time can be fired by a fast enough edge, through its own internal capacitance. A spike on the line or the electrical noise from a motor’s brushes can do it.

5.2 What the snubber does

Cs has to charge through Rs and the motor, so the voltage across the triac can rise no faster than that RC allows. The edge is slowed from a fraction of a microsecond to tens of microseconds. Rs limits the current when the triac fires and Cs dumps its charge into it, and it damps the ringing between Cs and the motor’s inductance. Typical values for a small motor are 0.1 µF (X2-rated, for use across the line) and a few hundred ohms to 1 kΩ. The donor board’s snubber is 1 kΩ and 0.1 µF.

A snubber has one cost: Cs passes current to the motor even with the triac off. At 60 Hz, 0.1 µF is about 27 kΩ, which lets about 4 mA through. That is enough to light a neon lamp but not to turn a motor. It does mean a snubbed control is never fully off; only a switch is. The VSM Base’s knee controller has one.

5.3 Snubberless triacs

Some triacs are built to switch inductive loads off without help. ST calls these “Snubberless” (its BW and CW versions), and NXP and WeEn call theirs “Hi-Com”. They are the three-quadrant types of §3. ST’s datasheet rates the BTA08-600BW, chosen for the MCU design in the speed-control paper, to turn off a current falling at 7 A/ms with no snubber, and to withstand 1,000 V/µs while off. A sewing motor’s current falls far more slowly than that. At 1 A RMS, its 1.4 A peak falls at no more than 2π×60×1.4≈0.532\pi \times 60 \times 1.4 \approx 0.53 A/ms. The price is a less sensitive gate: the BW version needs up to 50 mA to fire and fires only in quadrants I–III. The donor board’s BT136-600E is an ordinary sensitive-gate triac: it fires on 10 mA, its datasheet gives 50 V/µs static and no commutating figure, and the board carries a snubber.

5.4 Why fit one anyway

The MCU design uses a snubberless triac but leaves room for a snubber. There are three reasons it might be needed:

  • Noise. A universal motor’s brushes spark at every commutation, and the line carries spikes from other loads. The triac itself tolerates fast edges, but the opto-triac that fires it (a MOC3023) is wired from MT2 to the gate, so it sees the same edges. Its own datasheet adds a snubber to its application circuit for noisy environments.
  • Latching into an inductor. When the triac fires into an inductive load, its current starts from zero and rises slowly. It must pass the latching current (up to 70 mA for the BTA08-600BW) before the gate drive ends, or the triac drops out again. The MCU fires with a short pulse. At a late firing angle there is little voltage left to drive current through the motor’s inductance, so the current may not get there in time. A snubber helps, because Cs is charged to the voltage across the triac at the moment it fires. It discharges through Rs and the triac, giving a brief current of the order of an amp, enough to latch it. (The alternative is a longer gate pulse or a train of pulses, which firmware can supply.)
  • Interference. Slower edges radiate and conduct less noise.

So the plan is to build without a snubber, measure, and fit one if the triac turns on by itself or fails to latch.

6 The donor board, worked through

The VSM Base’s first knee controller reuses an inexpensive foot-pedal board, the XWW KB3151C (75 × 35 mm, labeled 110–120 V, 1.0 A), with a knee lever turning a pot in place of the pedal. The speed-control paper (§11 there) describes the controller and its mechanism. This section looks at the board’s circuit.

What is on it. It is §4’s minimal circuit with a few additions:

  • a BT136-600E triac, a sensitive-gate, four-quadrant part (§3), with a 1 kΩ and 0.1 µF snubber across it (§5);
  • a DB3 diac feeding the gate through R1 (1 kΩ), which limits the pulse;
  • the timing capacitor C2 (0.1 µF, X2-rated) charged through R2 (1 kΩ) from the wiper of a 200 kΩ linear slide pot, RV1;
  • a 2 MΩ trimmer, RV2, connected around the slide pot.

It is a two-terminal series device. It has only two spade tabs and sits in series in one leg of the motor circuit, with no separate mains input or motor output. That works because, as §4 showed, the timing network needs only the voltage across the triac. In the original pedal, only this control loop enters the box, as a two-wire lead from a standard cordset, and one pedal fits many machines.

At the end of the slide pot’s travel there is an off zone, where the wiper runs off the track and nothing fires. That is the pedal at rest.

6.1 The timing network and RV2

The board’s timing network is the one in §4’s figure, with one addition: the 2 MΩ trimmer RV2 is connected around the slide pot RV1 (200 kΩ). As traced, RV2 joins RV1’s pin 1, which is tied to MT2, to RV1’s pin-3 end. So current from MT2 can reach RV1’s wiper by two paths. One runs directly along RV1’s track from pin 1 to the wiper. The other runs through RV2 to pin 3, then back along the rest of the track to the wiper. The wiper feeds C2 through R2.

Which of RV1’s pins is the wiper is still to be checked with a meter. The algebra below doesn’t depend on it.

The parallel resistance. Let RR be RV1’s whole track (200 kΩ), aa the section from pin 1 to the wiper, and R−aR - a the rest. Let RvR_v be RV2’s setting, 0 to 2 MΩ. The direct path is aa, and the other is Rv+(R−a)R_v + (R - a). In parallel:

Req=a(Rv+R−a)Rv+RR_{eq} = \frac{a\,(R_v + R - a)}{R_v + R}

C2 (0.1 µF) charges through ReqR_{eq} plus R2 (1 kΩ). Pressing the pedal moves the wiper from the pin-3 end toward pin 1, so aa falls from RR to 0. Three things follow from the formula:

  • At full pedal, a=0a = 0 and Req=0R_{eq} = 0, whatever RV2 is set to. R2 alone sets the top speed.
  • At the start of the travel, just past the off zone, a=Ra = R and Req=RRv/(R+Rv)R_{eq} = R R_v / (R + R_v): RV1 and RV2 in parallel. This is RV2’s main effect. It lowers the largest timing resistance the pedal can reach, from RV1’s 200 kΩ toward zero.
  • In between, dReq/da=(Rv+R−2a)/(Rv+R)dR_{eq}/da = (R_v + R - 2a)/(R_v + R), which is zero at a=(Rv+R)/2a = (R_v + R)/2. If Rv≥RR_v \ge R, that point is at or past the end of the track. Then ReqR_{eq} rises steadily all the way back to the off zone, and the pedal is monotonic: less pedal, less speed. If Rv<RR_v < R, ReqR_{eq} peaks at (Rv+R)/4(R_v + R)/4 partway along the travel and falls again toward the off zone. At Rv=0R_v = 0 it becomes a(R−a)/Ra(R - a)/R, a parabola that is zero at both ends and 50 kΩ in the middle.

Firing. §4’s two thresholds turn these resistances into speeds. With C2 = 0.1 µF on 120 V, the motor starts when the timing resistance falls below about 137 kΩ, and it settles at about 125° firing, roughly 40% of the line’s RMS voltage. Once running, it keeps firing until the resistance rises past about 158 kΩ. The next figure runs the board’s network through the simulation of §4, pressing the pedal from rest and then easing back. It plots motor voltage as a stand-in for speed: at light load, a universal motor’s speed rises with its voltage, though not in proportion.

RV2 ReqR_{eq} at the start of travel Dead travel Voltage when it starts Lowest voltage while running
2 MΩ 182 kΩ 27% 38% 9%, at 15% of travel
1 MΩ 167 kΩ 21% 38% 7%, at 7% of travel
about 430 kΩ 137 kΩ none 39% 39%, at the off zone
200 kΩ 100 kΩ none 66% 66%
100 kΩ 67 kΩ none 83% 80%, a quarter of the way in
0 0 none 100% 90%, halfway

What a sewist notices. RV2 is the board’s minimum-speed adjustment, and turning it goes through four distinct behaviors.

  • Turned up, toward 2 MΩ. The first quarter of the pedal does nothing. Then the motor jumps on at about 40% of line voltage: a brisk start, not a crawl. Easing back, it slows further and keeps firing down to a tenth or less before it quits. Long before that, though, a sewing machine’s motor stalls or cogs, so the motor sets the practical floor. The feel is “it starts too fast, but slows if I let off”. After a stop, starting again needs the push again.
  • Turned down to about 430 kΩ. RV1 and RV2 in parallel then just match the start threshold. The motor starts as soon as the pedal leaves the off zone, at the same 40% or so, with no dead travel. Eased back, it keeps running at that speed right up to the off zone. This setting uses the whole pedal.
  • Turned further down. The motor starts at once, but at a higher minimum speed: 66% of line voltage at 200 kΩ. The low end is gone, and the pedal goes from off straight to a fast run.
  • Below RV1’s own 200 kΩ. The slowest point moves away from the start of the travel. At 100 kΩ the speed dips a little as the pedal goes down, then rises. Near zero the pedal is almost an on-off switch, faster at both ends of the travel than in the middle.

What RV2 cannot do is lower the snap-on speed. In every setting with dead travel, the motor starts at about 125° firing, near 40% of line voltage. RV2 only moves where in the travel that happens. The jump comes from the timing capacitor’s memory (§4), so a gentler start needs a different network, such as §4’s two-stage RC, not a different setting.

The start threshold also varies from board to board. A DB3’s breakover can be anywhere from 28 to 36 V, which alone moves the threshold from about 157 kΩ down to 121 kΩ. C2’s tolerance and the line voltage move it further. So the 430 kΩ setting is a model’s figure, not a dial position. That is why RV2 is a trimmer, set by ear: back it off until the motor just starts as the pedal leaves the off zone.

In the knee controller, the slide pot is replaced by the Bourns pot, wired as a two-terminal resistor, with RV1’s pin-3 pad jumpered to the wiper pad. That puts RV2 directly across the pot’s working section, so Req=a∥RvR_{eq} = a \parallel R_v, which always rises with aa. The off switch covers the dead travel up to the switch point, about 1” of knee travel. There the pot’s section is about 220 kΩ, and it falls to zero at full travel. With RV2 at 2 MΩ, the motor starts when aa falls to about 147 kΩ, a third of the way into the speed inch. At about 360 kΩ, which makes 220 kΩ ∥ RV2 = 137 kΩ, it starts as the switch closes. The same caveat applies: set it by ear.

7 Switches a gate can turn off

A thyristor can only be switched on; the circuit has to switch it off. That suits AC phase control, where the line does the switching off for free, and little else. Everything that chops DC, which includes every brake, every PWM motor drive and every inverter, needs a switch its control terminal can turn off as well as on. Three families do that job: bipolar transistors, power MOSFETs and IGBTs.

7.1 Bipolar transistors

A bipolar transistor conducts while current flows into its base, and stops when it doesn’t. That’s the turn-off a thyristor lacks, but it is expensive: a power transistor’s current gain is low, often 10 or 20, so switching 10 A takes most of an amp of continuous base drive. Darlington pairs raise the gain but add a volt or more of drop. Power bipolars ran the first transistor motor drives and switching supplies of the 1970s and 1980s. They have since been almost entirely replaced by the next two devices.

7.2 Power MOSFETs

A MOSFET’s gate is insulated from the channel by a thin oxide, so it draws no steady current. It is voltage-driven: about 10 V on the gate (4–5 V for a “logic-level” part) turns the channel fully on, and 0 V turns it off. The gate is a capacitor, so switching it takes a burst of current to move the gate charge, and a gate driver supplies that. Power MOSFETs reached the market in the late 1970s.

Its character:

  • On, it is a resistor, RDS(on)R_{DS(on)}. Conduction loss is I2RI^2 R. Low-voltage parts have resistances of a few milliohms, so at 24 V and tens of amps a MOSFET is nearly lossless. But RDS(on)R_{DS(on)} rises steeply with the voltage rating, roughly as its square in silicon, so at 600 V a MOSFET of the same size is a much poorer conductor.
  • It switches fast, in tens of nanoseconds. Switching losses stay small even at tens of kilohertz, which is why a MOSFET drive can run its PWM above hearing.
  • It has a built-in reverse diode, the body diode, from the way it is made. In a bridge that diode is the freewheeling path for an inductive load’s current when the MOSFET turns off.

MOSFETs rule at low voltage. A cordless drill’s speed trigger is a MOSFET switching the battery onto the motor at a few kilohertz, which is the whine Inside the Motor measured (§5 there). So is the H-bridge on the Pololu G2 board in the DC-motor variant of the MCU controller.

7.3 IGBTs

The insulated-gate bipolar transistor, developed in the early 1980s (notably by B. Jayant Baliga at General Electric), combines the two. A MOSFET section at the gate drives a bipolar structure underneath, built on an extra P layer. When it conducts, that layer floods the thick, lightly doped region that blocks the high voltage with carriers, a process called conductivity modulation, and the region’s resistance collapses.

  • On, it behaves like a diode drop, VCE(sat)V_{CE(sat)}, about 1.5–2 V, nearly independent of the voltage rating. Conduction loss is VCE(sat)×IV_{CE(sat)} \times I. At 600–1,700 V and tens of amps that beats a silicon MOSFET by a wide margin.
  • It is driven like a MOSFET, by gate voltage, with no steady gate current.
  • It turns off with a tail. The stored carriers have to recombine, so the current trails off over a microsecond or so after the gate goes low. That limits practical switching frequencies to a few kilohertz up to about 20–30 kHz, and it is the main switching loss.
  • It has no body diode. Inverter modules pair each IGBT with a separate fast diode for the freewheeling path.

IGBTs rule at mains-derived voltages and kilowatts:

  • Variable-frequency drives for induction motors (Inside the Motor, §7) are six IGBTs in a three-phase bridge, fed from rectified mains.
  • Industrial servo motors, including the “brushless servo” motors that have replaced clutch motors on industrial sewing machines, run on the same kind of bridge.
  • Induction cooktops, welders, electric vehicles and trains are all IGBT (or, increasingly, silicon carbide) machines.

7.4 Newer and older relatives

  • Silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) transistors are MOSFET-like switches in wide-bandgap materials. They block high voltage with a much thinner layer, so they combine MOSFET speed with low loss at high voltage. SiC is taking over electric-vehicle inverters, and GaN is what makes small USB-C chargers small.
  • Gate turn-off thyristors (GTOs) and IGCTs are thyristors built so that a large negative gate current can turn them off. They held the very-high-power end, locomotives and grid converters, before IGBTs grew large enough, and still do at the largest sizes.

7.5 Leading edge and trailing edge

A switch that can turn off allows a second way to chop the line. Leading-edge (forward-phase) control, the only kind a triac can do, starts conduction late in each half-cycle. Trailing-edge (reverse-phase) control starts at the zero and cuts off part way through. It needs a MOSFET or IGBT pair, one for each direction, or one inside a diode bridge.

Which suits a load depends on what it does at the edge:

  • Capacitive loads, such as the electronic drivers in many LED lamps, draw a spike of current when a leading-edge control switches the line on abruptly. A trailing-edge control lets the voltage rise with the sine instead, so dimmers for those lamps use it.
  • Inductive loads, such as a motor, are the opposite. Switching on abruptly is harmless, because the inductance limits how fast the current can rise. Cutting the current off abruptly is not: the inductance drives the voltage up until something conducts. A trailing-edge motor control therefore needs a path for that current, a freewheeling diode or a clamp, and on AC that is awkward. This is one reason AC motor speed controls have stayed with the triac.

On DC the freewheeling path is easy: a diode across the motor, or the body diodes of an H-bridge. With it, a transistor switch can chop the supply at any frequency and duty cycle, which is pulse-width modulation. The motor’s inductance smooths the current between pulses. Inside the Motor shows the waveforms (§5 there).

7.6 The families compared

SCR Triac Power MOSFET IGBT
Turned off by the circuit (current zero) the circuit (current zero) its gate its gate
Conducts one way both ways one way, plus body diode one way
Gate drive current pulse current pulse, either sign voltage, gate charge voltage, gate charge
On-state loss about 1–1.5 V drop about 1–1.5 V drop I2RDS(on)I^2 R_{DS(on)} about 1.5–2 V drop
Switching speed line frequency line frequency tens of ns; up to hundreds of kHz about 1 µs tail; up to tens of kHz
Typical home controlled rectifiers, big AC switches pedals, dimmers, appliance motors battery tools, DC drives, power supplies VFDs, servos, cooktops, EVs

8 Where each appears in the project

Every family in this paper turns up somewhere in the VSM Base’s controllers or in the controllers the speed-control paper compares.

  • The knee controller (speed-control paper §11) is the donor board of §6: a BT136 triac fired by a DB3 diac, leading-edge phase control, with a snubber. Its knee lever turns a pot in place of the slide pot, and a snap switch in series makes it fully off at rest, which a snubbed triac alone never is (§5).
  • The MCU phase controller (speed-control paper §11) uses a BTA08-600BW, a three-quadrant snubberless triac (§3, §5). A MOC3023 random-phase opto-triac fires it from the isolated microcontroller, and an H11AA1 optocoupler tells the microcontroller when the line crosses zero, so it can time the firing angle itself. A relay in series lets the firmware cut the motor whatever the triac is doing. There is room for a snubber, to be fitted only if testing shows the triac re-firing or failing to latch.
  • The rectified-DC variant puts the universal motor behind a diode bridge, with a freewheeling diode across it, and switches the bridge’s AC side with the same triac. The freewheeling diode lets the motor’s current continue between the triac’s pulses, so the current never stops and the triac’s commutation problem largely disappears.
  • The DC-motor variant drops the triac entirely. A 24 V supply feeds a Pololu G2 H-bridge, four MOSFETs (§7) switched at a PWM frequency above hearing, driving a “775” permanent-magnet motor. The body diodes carry the current when a MOSFET turns off, and the bridge can brake the motor actively, which no triac can.
  • The KB Electronics KBIC controllers (speed-control paper §8) are SCR bridges (§2) that turn the line into adjustable DC for a DC motor, with feedback from the armature voltage.
  • Variable-frequency drives and industrial servo motors (Inside the Motor, §7) are IGBT bridges (§7). The project doesn’t build one, but the clutch motor’s replacement on industrial machines is one.
